UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                               BEFORE THE
                 FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

    Joint Application for Authorization under
    Section 203 of the Federal Power Act of
    NextEra Energy, Inc., et al.                              Docket No. EC26-131-000



         PROTEST OF THE MARYLAND OFFICE OF PEOPLE’S COUNSEL

         The Maryland Office of People’s Counsel (“OPC”), pursuant to Rules 211 and 212

of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission

(“FERC” or “the Commission”), 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.211 and 385.212, submits this protest

in response to the Application for Authorization under Section 203(a)(1)(A) of the

Federal Power Act (the “Application”) filed by NextEra Energy, Inc. (“NextEra”) and

Dominion Energy, Inc. (“Dominion”) (together, “Applicants”). 1 OPC filed a timely and

unopposed motion for leave to intervene in this proceeding on August 12, 2026.

                                         *       *      *

         Applicants propose to place under one corporate parent over 10 million customer

accounts, 110 gigawatts (“GW”) of generation capacity, extensive transmission and

distribution lines serving a region experiencing skyrocketing data center-driven demand,

and the nation’s largest stock of renewable and battery storage assets. This massive

concentration of power in a single company jeopardizes regional transmission



1
 Application for Authorization Under Section 203 of the Federal Power Act and Requests for
Confidential Treatment and Limited Waivers of Certain Filing Requirements, Docket No. EC26-131-000
(July 15, 2026) (“Application”).
 competition, risks undue influence over independent Regional Transmission Organization

(“RTO”) processes, and portends increased consolidation by the company’s current rivals.

For these reasons, as explained in this protest, the Commission should deny the

Application as inconsistent with the public interest.



                                       BACKGROUND

       OPC is the statutory representative of the residential ratepayers of utility services

in Maryland. Pursuant to Maryland Code Annotated, Public Utilities Article, Section

2-205(b), the People’s Counsel “may appear before any federal or state [agency] as

necessary to protect the interests of residential […] users of [gas, electricity or other

regulated services].” OPC regularly protests transactions proposed to this Commission

under Section 203 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) when a transaction risks

anti-competitive conduct that could harm Maryland consumers.

       Applicants, collectively, own electric distribution, transmission, and generation

assets located within the operating footprint of PJM Interconnection, LLC (“PJM”), the

RTO that administers the regional electric transmission grid and wholesale electric

markets supplying the State of Maryland. 2 PJM is regulated by the Commission.3

Applicant, Dominion, owns and operates generation facilities and develops and owns

transmission lines which sell and transmit electric energy into and through markets




2
 OPC participates in PJM stakeholder processes as a member of the End-Use Customer sector.
3
 See Order No. 2000, Regional Transmission Organizations, 89 FERC ¶ 61,285 (1999) (“Order No.
2000”).
                                                2
 administered by PJM.4 Applicant, NextEra, is a transmission developer that competes

with incumbent developers like Dominion to build and operate transmission lines within

PJM’s footprint, including in Maryland. 5 NextEra also owns generation facilities in

PJM’s footprint and has significant planned generation development in the region. 6



                                             PROTEST

        The Commission may approve a proposed transaction only if it finds that the

transaction “will be consistent with the public interest.” 7 The Commission should fulfill

its full statutory mandate to evaluate the public interest in this transaction by requiring

that Applicants meet a more inclusive standard than mere avoidance of harm to

pre-merger competition. Under the statutorily required standard, the Commission must

find that the transaction’s potential to harm regional transmission competition, RTO

independence, and long-term competition is grounds for rejection of the Application.

  Application at 9-10.
5

the MidAtlantic Resiliency Link, would include transmission facilities in Maryland. See Press Release,
NextEra Energy Transmission MidAtlantic, Inc., The MidAtlantic Resiliency Link Moves into Next Phase
(Jan. 30, 2026), https://www.midatlanticresiliencylink.com/hubfs/midatlantic-resiliencylink-news-release-
jan-2026.pdf.
6

Herald-Standard (Sept. 9, 2026), https://www.heraldstandard.com/news/local_news/2026/sep/09/13-
billion-power-plant-proposed-in-fayette-county/.
7
  16 U.S.C. § 824b(a)(4).

 I.      The FPA’s public interest standard requires the Commission to evaluate the
        transaction’s harm to consumers and long-term competition.

        Section 203 of the FPA requires the Commission to determine whether Applicants’

proposed transaction is consistent with the public interest. 8 The Commission ordinarily

finds the public interest met if a transaction “produce[s] no detriment overall.” 9 That is,

Applicants need not demonstrate to the Commission any benefits to competition or

consumers.10 The Commission errs in construing the public interest so narrowly.

        Despite its approval of over 80 mergers and acquisitions since the mid-1980s, the

Commission has never clearly defined the public interest it protects. 11 Congress has. Its

purposes in passing the FPA were to “curb abusive practices by public utilities and to

protect customers from excessive rates and charges” and to maintain competition “to the

maximum extent possible.”12 Mergers that conflict with those purposes are necessarily

not “consistent with the public interest.” This unprecedented transaction is the

Commission’s chance to align its merger decision-making with Congress’s mandate. The

Commission is not bound by its more recent permissive approvals. In defining the public



8
  Id.
9
  Midwest Power Sys., 71 FERC ¶ 61,386, 62,513 (1995); See generally Jodi L. Short, In Search of the
Public Interest, 40 Yale J. on Reg. 759, 810-11 (2023) (explaining that FERC’s public interest analysis
rarely engages in cost-benefit analysis or references net benefits for consumers).
10
   Utah Power & Light Co., 47 FERC ¶ 61,209, 61,750 (1989) (“Applicants […] need not show a positive
benefit of the merger.”).
11
   Scott Hempling, Inconsistent with the Public Interest: FERC’s Three Decades of Deference to
Electricity Consolidation, 39 Energy L.J. 233, 268 (2018) (“In none of FERC’s merger issuances […] is
there a clear definition of public interest[.]”); see also Jodi Short, supra note 9, at 806 (“FERC rarely
makes explicit claims about the scope of its discretion under Section 203, and I found no bald claims of
broad discretion.”).
12
   Fla. Power & Light Co. v. Fed. Energy Reg. Comm’n., 617 F.2d 809, 816 (1980) (quoting Gulf States
Utilities Co. v. FPC, 411 U.S. 747, 758 (1973) and Alexandria v. Fed. Power Comm’n., 555 F.2d 1020,
1022 (1977)); Otter Tail Power Co. v. United States, 410 U.S. 366, 374 (1973).
                                                    4
 interest as requiring the promotion of effective competition, the Commission would act

with the necessary fidelity to the purposes of its enabling statute and need only

acknowledge and explain a change in practice. 13

        Congress’s mandate requires that Section 203 transactions benefit consumers and

long-term competition. Applicants hope that the Commission will ignore its mandate. The

statute forbids that result. Congress vested the Commission with its public interest

mandate to “prevent the notorious investment and profit abuses which had developed in

the [utility] industry under the domination of holding companies.” 14 Indeed, Section

203’s public interest mandate “carrie[d] with it the duty to deny an application […] when

it cannot be shown that […] the consuming public will be benefitted thereby.” 15 The scale

of Applicants’ proposed transaction and its potential harm to consumers and long-term

competition demand the Commission bring to bear the full measure of its authority in its

review.


II.     The proposed transaction would harm competitive transmission development
        in the PJM region.

        Transmission lines have significant implications for competition and consumers.

Recognizing that “[u]tilities owning or controlling transmission facilities possess



13
   See Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 394 (2024) (“[O]f course, [a] statute’s meaning
may well be that the agency is authorized to exercise a degree of discretion. Congress has often enacted
such statutes[.]”); Verizon v. FCC, 740 F.3d 623, 636 (2014) (“[R]easoned decision-making ordinarily
demands that an agency acknowledge and explain the reasons for a changed interpretation.”).
14
   In re Dairyland Power Coop., 37 FPC 12, 15 (1967) (explaining that Title II of the Federal Water
Power Act, which added the Commission’s public interest standard for approving utility mergers, was
included as part of the same bill as Title I of the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 and
therefore the statutes share a common purpose).
15
   Inland Power & Light Co., 1 FPC 380, 384-85 (1937).
                                                    5
 substantial market power […] and will […] exercise that market power in order to […]

deny their wholesale customers access to competitively priced electric generation,” the

Commission has sought to encourage robust competition. 16 FERC Order No. 1000

requires RTOs to consider competitors to these incumbent developers of transmission

projects on a non-discriminatory basis, and in doing so, it created opportunities for

non-incumbents to finance projects through cost-of-service rates. 17 These non-incumbent

developers allow lower-cost, distantly generated electricity to compete with incumbent

local facilities to serve consumer demand. 18

       Despite FERC’s rules, very few regional transmission projects have been

competitively bid.19 However, NextEra, a non-incumbent transmission developer, has

successfully bid on two major projects in recent PJM procurements. In 2023, NextEra

won the right to build over 100 miles of 550 kilovolt (“kV”) lines through Pennsylvania,

https://www.npr.org/transcripts/1197967999 (“One study found only three to 8% of all transmission

 Maryland, Virginia, and West Virginia.20 NextEra is also the 75 percent equity backer of a

project selected by PJM in 2026 to build over 200 miles of 765 kV lines through

Pennsylvania and West Virginia.21 Dominion competes with NextEra for projects in PJM

and submitted bids for major projects in the solicitations that led to the above-referenced

NextEra projects.22 Dominion’s transmission footprint includes nearly 7,000 miles of

transmission primarily in the PJM region, with plans to add approximately $4.8 billion in

recently approved competitively bid projects in the region. 23

       Approval of Applicants’ proposed transaction will significantly reduce competition

for regional transmission projects. The probable consequence of fewer companies

competing for fewer regional projects is increased transmission prices for consumers.

Competition is thus critical to achieving cost discipline in the transmission market. In

2025, approximately 50 percent of transmission spending went to local projects that are

not subject to meaningful cost review by RTOs, FERC, or the states, including

 Maryland.24 As these “supplemental” local projects increase transmission capacity they

obviate the need for cost-effective regional transmission allocated through RTO-

administered competitive bidding.25 In evaluating Applicants’ proposed transaction, the

Commission must account for the true market impacts of consolidation among

transmission rivals and the resulting inefficiencies in transmission planning.


III.    The proposed transaction risks creating a conglomerate that could exercise
        undue influence over RTO decisions.

        In encouraging the formation of RTOs, the Commission has sought to rein in

utilities’ anti-competitive development of transmission that can impose unjust and

unreasonable transmission costs passed on to consumers. 26 RTOs like PJM make

decisions through pseudo-democratic processes and stakeholder consultation and

collaboration that ideally produce independent decision-making. The Commission

reviews RTO governance structures with an eye towards ensuring that incumbents cannot

exert undue influence over RTO decisions.27




24

(June 22, 2026), https://www.brattle.com/insights-events/publications/annual-us-transmission-

https://opc.maryland.gov/Portals/0/Files/Publications/Rising%20Transmission%20Costs%202026-03-
25%20CORRECTED%20FINAL.pdf.
25

26

27

         The Commission must consider how consolidation undermines the “bedrock”

principle of independence for RTOs as it reviews Applicants’ proposed transaction. 28 For

example, powerful conglomerates have the legal and regulatory budgets to ensure their

teams of lawyers and experts can actively participate in hundreds of RTO sub-working

group meetings a year.29 For smaller market participants with limited resources, this

resource asymmetry may result in less say over RTO policy development. 30 What is

more, in RTOs like PJM, large holding companies can and do direct their subsidiaries to

vote in the interests of the parent, even when such a vote may run counter to the interests

of the subsidiary’s operating sector.31

        Further, the threat of a utility conglomerate withdrawing from an RTO creates

leverage over RTO decisions and processes. RTOs operate the assets of large

transmission and generation owners for the efficient management of regional markets.

However, owners’ participation is voluntary.


28
   Id. at PP 199-200 (“In the NOPR, the Commission reiterated its earlier statement that ‘the principle of
independence is the bedrock upon which the ISO must be built’ and that this standard should apply to all
RTOs”).
29

30

https://www.monitoringanalytics.com/filings/2016/IMM_Comments_Docket_No_RM16-21-
000_20161212.pdf (“Whether horizontal mergers join generation or transmission companies, the
affiliation of multiple operating companies enhances the voting weight and influence of the combined
company in the RTO stakeholder process.”); See also Christina Simeone, PJM Governance: Can Reforms

https://kleinmanenergy.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/PJM-Governance-Reforms-1.pdf.

         As the Independent Market Monitor for PJM has observed, “[t]he greater the

proportion of the RTO’s assets represented by the transmission owner, the greater the

threat of exit to the RTO and the greater the potential influence of the transmission owner

over the RTO governance and processes.” 32 While some states now require utilities in

their jurisdictions to join RTOs, utilities retain the ability—even if just a threat—to

switch or form a new RTO.33 Applicants’ combined footprint spans a major portion of the

Southeastern United States, the Southwest Power Pool, Inc., and the PJM operating area,

increasing the potential for the merged company to exercise significant exit leverage. The

threat of exit, given Applicants’ combined scale and the importance of their participation

to any RTO’s operations, warrants close scrutiny by the Commission.


IV.     The proposed transaction risks further regional consolidation.

        Individual mergers have cumulative effects. However, the Commission has for

decades disclaimed its authority to interrogate whether an individual transaction may lead

to future consolidation.34 Despite antitrust considerations being core to the Commission’s

merger reviews, it neglects antitrust law’s powerful means of preventing runaway




32
   Independent Market Monitor for PJM, Application of Exelon Corporation and Pepco Holdings, Inc.,
Comments of the Independent Market Monitor for PJM (Docket No. EC14-96-000, July 21, 2014), at 6,
https://www.monitoringanalytics.com/filings/2014/IMM_Comment_EC14-96-000_20140721.pdf.
33
   See generally Nat’l Conf. of State Legis., Electric Transmission Development: The Role of States (Jan.
20, 2026), https://www.ncsl.org/energy/electric-transmission-development-the-role-of-states.
34
   See generally Duke Energy Corp., 113 FERC ¶ 61,297, 62,200 (2005) (“We reject [the] argument that
the Commission should analyze the instant merger not only on its own specific terms but as a harbinger of
change. […] [W]e cannot deny […] a proposed merger based on speculation about general trends that
may or may not occur in the future.”).
                                                   10
 consolidation—incipiency doctrine. 35 Since the 1960s, competition enforcers have

applied this doctrine to arrest trends toward concentration in their incipiency rather than

focusing only on existing market conditions. 36 The results of the Commission reviewing

mergers without a focus on incipiency are telling.

         The Commission’s continuous approval of mergers since the 1980s has reduced

the number of independent investor-owned utilities from several hundred to 17. 37 Indeed,

consolidation has accelerated as holding companies have acquired one another, with ten

holding companies now owning nearly half of all formerly independent utilities. 38

Maryland has seen widespread consolidation of its electric utilities since the early 2000s,

including FirstEnergy’s 2010 acquisition of Potomac Edison and Exelon’s acquisition of

Baltimore Gas & Electric in 2012 and Pepco Holdings in 2016, which was itself the result

of the 2002 merger of Potomac Electric Power Co. (“Pepco”) and Delmarva Power &

Light.

         Applicants seek Commission approval to create “the world’s largest regulated

electric utility business […] and one of the world’s largest energy infrastructure

companies.”39 It is incumbent upon the Commission to evaluate the merger’s impacts on

and anticompetitive issues by [FERC], moreover, serves the important function of establishing a first line

36

37
   Hempling, supra note 11, at 252 (Note that since this article’s publication, one of the formerly

38

https://newsroom.nexteraenergy.com/2026-05-18-NextEra-Energy-and-Dominion-Energy-to-Combine,-
                                                    11
 long-term competition. Instead of accepting Applicants’ promises of increased efficiency

and innovation, the Commission should adopt from the incipiency doctrine a presumption

against mergers that would harm resilient redundancy (i.e., enough competition to control

for unpredictable loss of another competitor in a relevant market). 40 Such a standard

would protect against both the potential failure of any remedies imposed on the

transaction and any individual merger starting or furthering a wave of additional mergers

that cumulatively harm competition.41

        Applicants’ transaction risks exactly this type of merger wave. NextEra seeks

ownership and control over Dominion’s regulated operations and capture of explosive

forecasted data center-driven electricity demand.42 In forming the largest utility

conglomerate in the country, regional competitors like American Electric Power (“AEP”),

Exelon, and FirstEnergy all have increased justifications to seek a similar merger. 43 For

 example, a transmission- and generation-first company like AEP could seek a deal with

FirstEnergy or Exelon, which, similar to Dominion, distribute electricity where data

center development is increasing. While projected data center demand may never

materialize, and so too the efficiencies promised in Applicants’ proposed transaction and

any hypothetical follow-on deals, competition in PJM would be severely and irreversibly

reduced.44

                                                CONCLUSION

        The Commission should reject Applicants’ proposed transaction as inconsistent

with the public interest. Applicants’ merger would suppress competitive transmission

development in PJM at a time when competitive bidding for transmission expansion is

already scarce. The transaction would also concentrate influence over PJM’s governance,

undermining independent, non-discriminatory RTO decision-making. Further, the

transaction risks setting in motion follow-on consolidation among remaining regional

competitors. The Commission should not evaluate this unprecedented transaction by the

deferential standard Applicants invite it to apply. Rather, the Commission must exercise

its authority under Section 203 and account for the transaction’s lack of consumer benefit

and long-term effects on competition.
